frame.speaker: Ugraśravas, speaking to the sages
notes: Ugraśravas arrives at Śaunaka’s gathering in Naimiṣa. Asked where he has come from, he says he heard Vaiśampāyana tell Vyāsa’s stories at King Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice.

The war belongs to the past of these two gatherings. The atlas follows selected scenes in the order of the reading. It pauses here for the frame and later marks another interruption when Bṛhadaśva tells Yudhiṣṭhira about Nala.

vow.speaker: Devavrata
notes: The fisherman’s concern is succession. Devavrata gives up the throne for Satyavatī’s future children, but the fisherman still worries that Devavrata’s sons could assert a claim.

Devavrata therefore vows to remain celibate. This secures Śāntanu’s marriage and makes the inheritance depend on Satyavatī’s line. The man later called Bhīṣma continues to protect the house he has promised never to rule.

lac.speaker: Yudhiṣṭhira, speaking to Bhīma
notes: Yudhiṣṭhira smells the fat and lac in the building and tells Bhīma why he suspects it can be set alight. He decides that they should appear unworried while secretly preparing to leave.
Vidura’s help enables an escape through a tunnel. The fire also kills other occupants. The court’s belief that the Pāṇḍavas have died makes their later appearance in Pañcāla a political surprise.

draupadi.speaker: Vaiśampāyana
notes: Drupada sets a trial of archery. The Pāṇḍavas attend in disguise, and Arjuna strikes the target through the apparatus. Draupadī approaches the successful archer.

The princes challenge the outcome. Arjuna and Bhīma defend it, and the revelation that the brothers survived the fire changes Drupada’s relationship to the Kuru house. The marriage arrangements unfold in later chapters.

new-capital.speaker: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, addressing the Pāṇḍavas
notes: Dhṛtarāṣṭra tells the returning brothers to take a share of the realm and live at Khāṇḍavaprastha. The episode offers a political solution to the cousins’ rivalry by giving the brothers a separate seat.
The new city is called Indraprastha. Once Yudhiṣṭhira has a court and standing of his own, the dice match in Sabhā puts the resources and authority acquired there at risk.

dice.speaker: Vaiśampāyana, with the court’s speakers named below
notes: Śakuni plays on Duryodhana’s behalf. As Yudhiṣṭhira’s assets run out, Śakuni repeatedly prompts him to name another stake. After the king loses himself, Śakuni suggests staking Draupadī to win his freedom back.

Draupadī refuses to accept the messenger’s report as a ruling. Her question makes the order of the final two stakes decisive. If Yudhiṣṭhira no longer had authority over himself, what authority could he claim over her?

Dhṛtarāṣṭra grants boons that release the brothers. The court then recalls them for a second game. The loser must spend twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth incognito, with the forest term renewed if discovered.
dice.edition: The Sanskrit locators and the wager sequence here follow the Critical Edition. English summaries are editorial paraphrases. Ganguli’s translation uses a separate section numbering system.

exile-start.speaker: Vaiśampāyana
notes: The Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī leave after the second dice game. The terms asserted in the assembly now govern their movements, and the risk of recognition will shape the thirteenth year.

In the forest Yudhiṣṭhira asks who has suffered as he has. Bṛhadaśva answers with an older story about another king who lost at dice. The invitation to hear Nala arises from the exile, while Nala’s story has its own time and setting.

nala.speaker: Bṛhadaśva, speaking to Yudhiṣṭhira
notes: Nala and Damayantī marry, but Nala loses his kingdom to Puṣkara at dice. In exile he abandons Damayantī, who survives by seeking shelter and eventually devises a way to bring him within reach again.
The reunion depends on recognition, exchange of skills, and a second match in which Nala recovers his kingdom. When Bṛhadaśva finishes, the text returns to Yudhiṣṭhira and his own unresolved exile.

hidden-year.speaker: Yudhiṣṭhira and the exiles
notes: Before entering Virāṭa’s court the exiles choose roles. Yudhiṣṭhira becomes Kaṅka, a dice player, and Arjuna becomes Bṛhannaḍā, a teacher of dance and music. Draupadī serves in the queen’s household.
When the cattle are driven off, Prince Uttara needs a charioteer. Bṛhannaḍā takes that role, bringing the concealment that has kept the exiles safe into tension with the defence of the kingdom.

peace.speaker: Duryodhana, answering Kṛṣṇa
notes: Kṛṣṇa comes as envoy. Duryodhana refuses to yield even the ground that the point of a needle could pierce. The speech makes explicit that an agreement requires a concession he will not make.
The refusal closes the path to a settlement in this reading. The setting moves from the court of Hastināpura to the armies gathered at Kurukṣetra.

karna-loyalty.speaker: Karṇa answers Kuntī
notes: Kuntī asks Karṇa to recognise his brothers and join them. Karṇa points out that she left him as a child and approaches him now when his change of side would help the Pāṇḍavas. He argues that leaving Duryodhana in wartime would betray people who have placed their trust in him.

He promises to spare four brothers but excludes Arjuna from the promise. Kuntī will have five sons, he says, whether he or Arjuna dies. At the water rites after the battle the other brothers learn what she knew.

omens.speaker: Vyāsa, speaking to Dhṛtarāṣṭra
notes: Vyāsa reports disturbing sights to the king before Sañjaya’s battle narration. At 6.2.31 he describes Arundhatī in relation to Vasiṣṭha. The next verses and chapter include other celestial disturbances.

Oak reads the relationship as which star crosses the meridian first. That reading adds a specific observing rule to the passage. The modern observer map and the illustrative two-star lesson let you inspect the geometry separately.

gita.speaker: Sañjaya reports the exchange between Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa
notes: At Arjuna’s request, Kṛṣṇa stops between the armies. Arjuna recognizes his own family and teachers among the people he would have to kill. By the end of the opening chapter he has set down his bow.

Arjuna then asks for instruction. The dialogue considers action, duty, discipline, knowledge and devotion. Its final chapter returns to the practical choice: Arjuna says his confusion has lifted and he will act.

bhishma-falls.speaker: Sañjaya
notes: On the tenth day the Pāṇḍavas put Śikhaṇḍin in front. Bhīṣma will not strike at Śikhaṇḍin, and Arjuna uses that opening to shoot him.
The arrows support Bhīṣma’s body when he falls. His command ends, but the man himself survives long enough to teach after the war. That interval later becomes part of the dating discussion.

drona-commands.speaker: Duryodhana asks Karṇa for advice
notes: Duryodhana says an army can no more fight without a leader than a ship can move safely without a helmsman. He asks Karṇa to name the successor to Bhīṣma, who has led the army for ten days.
Karṇa proposes their teacher Droṇa. An alliance formed in the Kuru training ground now divides teacher from former students, and the new commander makes capturing Yudhiṣṭhira a goal.

abhimanyu.speaker: Sañjaya
notes: Droṇa forms an array the Pāṇḍavas cannot break without Arjuna. Abhimanyu says he can enter, and Yudhiṣṭhira promises that others will follow. Jayadratha holds them back after Abhimanyu breaks through.
Several warriors attack Abhimanyu, and he is killed after losing his chariot and weapons. When Arjuna learns what happened, he binds himself to kill Jayadratha the following day.

jayadratha.speaker: Sañjaya, reporting Kṛṣṇa’s instruction
notes: Jayadratha is guarded until sunset because Arjuna has set himself that deadline. Kṛṣṇa tells Arjuna when to strike and tells him how to direct the severed head.
The story gives the darkness a role in Kṛṣṇa’s strategy. Treating the passage as a solar eclipse requires a separate textual assumption and a test for local visibility.
jayadratha.edition: Ganguli’s Droṇa Parva CXLV is a separately numbered translation. Compare it with BORI 7.121; the edition labels must travel with the references.

drona-dies.speaker: Sañjaya
notes: Bhīma has killed an elephant called Aśvatthāman and announces the death. Droṇa seeks confirmation from Yudhiṣṭhira, who gives a misleading answer by letting the report of a death carry farther than the qualification about the elephant.

Droṇa finally lays down his weapons after Bhīma addresses him. Dhṛṣṭadyumna seizes the opening. In the last parva Indra brings the misleading answer back as the reason Yudhiṣṭhira was shown a place of suffering.

karna-commands.speaker: Dhṛtarāṣṭra asks how Karṇa began his command
notes: After Droṇa falls, the defeated Kaurava leaders return to camp. Duryodhana adopts Karṇa’s plan and orders the army to make ready.
The preparations begin in the last part of the night, before Karṇa leads the remaining force into battle. The famous duel with Arjuna belongs to the second day of Karṇa’s command.

karna.speaker: Kṛṣṇa answers Karṇa
notes: When Karṇa’s chariot wheel sinks he appeals to the rules of battle and asks Arjuna to wait. Kṛṣṇa asks where Karṇa’s concern for dharma was during the wrongs done to Draupadī and the Pāṇḍavas.
Arjuna kills Karṇa. The exchange tests whether a warrior can invoke a rule when he needs its protection after helping deny it to others. The army passes to Śalya on the last day.

maces.speaker: Sañjaya
notes: Bhīma strikes Duryodhana on the thighs, fulfilling the threat he made after the humiliation in the assembly. Balarāma objects that a mace blow below the waist violates the rules.
The combat ends but the argument over the victory continues. Duryodhana’s last supporters survive the duel and take the war into the sleeping camp.

night-raid.speaker: Vaiśampāyana
notes: Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman go to the Pāṇḍava camp at night. Aśvatthāman enters while the others guard the exits. Among those killed are Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin and Draupadī’s sons.
The attack follows the last day of open fighting. It changes what victory means for the surviving Pāṇḍavas and leads to the confrontation over Aśvatthāman’s weapon later in the book.

mourning.speaker: Gāndhārī, addressing Kṛṣṇa
notes: The women of the Kuru houses see the bodies of their relatives. Gāndhārī turns her grief into an accusation: Kṛṣṇa had the power to intervene while the two branches destroyed each other.
She tells him that his own kin will destroy one another and their women will mourn in the same way. His answer accepts their eventual destruction. Mausala takes up that prediction.

karna-revealed.speaker: Kuntī speaks to the Pāṇḍavas
notes: When the families make water offerings for their dead, Kuntī tells her sons to include Karṇa. The warrior they remember as Duryodhana’s ally was her firstborn and their elder brother.

Yudhiṣṭhira grieves and asks why she kept the secret. He makes the offering and brings Karṇa’s wives to the rites. A ritual for those the brothers already counted as kin now makes them acknowledge someone they fought as an enemy.

rule.speaker: Bhīṣma teaches Yudhiṣṭhira
notes: Bhīṣma asks the new king to work at governing instead of relying on fortune. He allows that both effort and fate matter but puts effort first because a ruler can act on it.

He makes truth the basis of trust between a king and others. That teaching comes after a war in which Yudhiṣṭhira himself used a misleading answer against Droṇa. The last parva will return to that act.

crisis.speaker: Yudhiṣṭhira asks about the duties of distress
notes: Yudhiṣṭhira asks how a king can survive when the treasury is exhausted, his advisers are unreliable, and a stronger opponent attacks. Bhīṣma treats the question as difficult because a course defensible in an emergency may be rejected in ordinary life.

He discusses using resources temporarily and granting relief later. In the next chapter he considers a treaty with the stronger side and, if necessary, abandoning the capital. Surviving the crisis makes rebuilding possible.

liberation.speaker: A son answers his father in a story told by Bhīṣma
notes: Yudhiṣṭhira asks what is worth doing when time wears away all living things. Bhīṣma tells him about a son who asks his father a similar question. His father describes a succession of duties: study, raise a family, perform rites, and finally live in the forest.

The son asks why it is safe to wait. Death and ageing advance each day, he says. He urges his father to do what is good while the chance to act remains. Bhīṣma lets a younger person challenge the inherited sequence instead of delivering the advice in his own voice.

giving.speaker: Bhīṣma recounts Nārada’s teaching
notes: Yudhiṣṭhira asks what a ruler can give that will do the most good. In one exchange Bhīṣma praises a gift of land because it continues to support crops, animals and livelihood.

The next question prompts him to retell Nārada’s praise of food. Giving something that sustains life can matter immediately. The two chapters place rulership’s durable resources beside a person’s most immediate need.

bhishma-dies.speaker: Bhīṣma, speaking to those gathered at his death
notes: Yudhiṣṭhira returns to Bhīṣma. The passage refers to the sun’s northward turn, and Bhīṣma counts fifty-eight nights lying on the arrows and names the month Māgha.
The story ends his role as teacher and elder. Reading these lines as a calendar constraint involves deciding which interval the nights measure and how the month and seasonal terms are related.

horse.speaker: Vaiśampāyana
notes: The released horse extends the restored royal court’s dealings with other kings. At Maṇipura, Babhruvāhana welcomes his father Arjuna, who treats the welcome as a failure to challenge the horse’s escort.

Ulūpī urges Babhruvāhana to fight. The encounter brings the claim of sovereignty into conflict with kinship, and Ulūpī later restores Arjuna after he falls. The story of rebuilding the kingdom revisits violence inside a family.

retreat.speaker: Nārada brings news to Yudhiṣṭhira
notes: Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī leave the court, and Kuntī goes with them. Their withdrawal takes three senior figures out of the kingdom the Pāṇḍavas have rebuilt.
Nārada later tells Yudhiṣṭhira of the forest fire. Dhṛtarāṣṭra tells Sañjaya to escape. He, Gāndhārī and Kuntī remain, and the news returns the story to the duty of mourning.

dvaraka.speaker: Vaiśampāyana
notes: After the Yādavas kill one another, Arjuna comes to Dvārakā and tries to lead survivors out. The book describes the sea covering the city after they leave.
Gāndhārī’s prediction from Strī has reached its narrative outcome. Arjuna’s difficulty protecting the survivors makes him confront the loss of powers that served him at Kurukṣetra.

ascent.speaker: Yudhiṣṭhira answers Indra
notes: The brothers leave the kingdom to Parikṣit. Draupadī and four of the brothers fall along the journey. Bhīma asks Yudhiṣṭhira why each has fallen before falling himself.
Indra offers Yudhiṣṭhira a place in heaven but tells him to leave the dog behind. Yudhiṣṭhira refuses to abandon a dependent companion for his own reward. The dog reveals itself as Dharma.

last-test.speaker: Indra explains the test
notes: Yudhiṣṭhira has seen Duryodhana in heaven and heard the voices of his own family in a place of suffering. He chooses to remain where they are when their voices say his presence brings relief.

Indra links Yudhiṣṭhira’s experience to the deceptive way Droṇa was told about his son. Dharma recognizes his decision to stay with his family. The closing test carries a choice made on the battlefield into the epic’s final account of loyalty and truth.

wagers: Yudhiṣṭhira names his stores of gold.
He wagers the chariot that brought them to the hall and its horses.
He wagers the elephants equipped for royal service and battle.
He stakes the numerous women who serve his household and guests.
Next are the men who serve guests in the royal household.
The stake includes chariots, teams of horses and paid chariot warriors.
He puts up the horses Citraratha gave Arjuna.
He names massed chariots, carts, horses and their men.
Four hundred stores of worked gold finish this series. Vidura speaks in the next chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira names counted sums and puts his wealth in play again.
Cattle, horses, goats and sheep enter the stakes.
The wager names territory, resources and people, with exceptions for Brahmins and their property.
Yudhiṣṭhira stakes the jewellery worn by the princes.
Śakuni then goads the king by comparing Mādrī’s sons with Arjuna and Bhīma.
Yudhiṣṭhira calls him Phalguna and recalls the help he gives in battle.
The king wagers his fourth brother.
He loses after offering his own service.
Śakuni suggests this stake after Yudhiṣṭhira has lost himself. Śakuni declares it won at 2.58.43.
court: Asks whether Yudhiṣṭhira lost himself before he wagered her.
Sets two premises in tension: a man without property cannot stake another’s goods, yet a wife is held to be under a husband’s authority. He declines to decide.
Distinguishes the wager of Draupadī from the losses of property and brothers. Arjuna urges him to restrain his anger toward Yudhiṣṭhira.
Judges her unwon. He cites the king’s prior loss, the manipulation of the game, and her marriage to all five brothers.
Takes the elders’ silence as support for the wager and disputes Vikarṇa’s reading.
Proposes the terms of the second game to Dhṛtarāṣṭra. The challenge replaces the temporary release with a threat of exile.

warDays.event: Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to stop the chariot between the armies. The dialogue ends with Arjuna ready to act.
After the first day’s withdrawal, Yudhiṣṭhira fears defeat. The Pāṇḍavas deploy a crane-shaped formation. Duryodhana responds by drawing his commanders together against it.
As the Pāṇḍava lines scatter, Kṛṣṇa leaves his chariot with his discus and rushes at Bhīṣma. Arjuna catches and restrains him, then renews his own attack.
Bhīma breaks the elephant force. Duryodhana orders the other troops to concentrate on him, turning an elephant attack into a wider assault.
Śikhaṇḍin and Virāṭa confront Bhīṣma. The encounter brings Śikhaṇḍin against the commander before the two sides use that pairing decisively on day 10.
Duryodhana’s brothers surround Bhīma, whom Sañjaya compares to the sun surrounded by planets. The fighting follows Sañjaya’s warning to Dhṛtarāṣṭra that the war follows from the dice game.
Bhīṣma forms the Kaurava array at sunrise. As Arjuna disrupts their side’s ranks, Duryodhana rallies the Kaurava warriors and Bhīṣma moves to oppose him.
Bhīṣma leads a formation compared to an ocean, with Droṇa and Bhagadatta behind him. After heavy losses Duryodhana consults his allies that evening about defeating the Pāṇḍavas.
The army reassembles after Duryodhana and Bhīṣma’s difficult conversation. After the day’s damage the Pāṇḍavas seek Bhīṣma’s advice, and he tells them how to bring him down.
Śikhaṇḍin fronts the attack. Arjuna brings Bhīṣma down, ending his command.
Duryodhana asks Karṇa to name a successor and Droṇa takes command. Droṇa makes capturing Yudhiṣṭhira a priority, but Arjuna’s presence frustrates him.
Arjuna hears Bhagadatta’s elephants breaking the ranks and turns toward the main battle. Bhagadatta falls in their encounter, while Droṇa’s effort to capture Yudhiṣṭhira goes on.
Abhimanyu enters the battle formation. His death leads to Arjuna’s vow to kill Jayadratha.
Arjuna pursues Jayadratha before sunset and kills him. The next stretch of the battle runs into the night.
Droṇa dies on his fifth day in command. The deceptive report about his son returns in Yudhiṣṭhira’s final test.
Karṇa takes command and assembles the surviving army at dawn. The first day of his command ends with both forces still in the field for a final duel the next day.
The text names the seventeenth day. Karṇa’s death in the duel ends his command.
Śalya leads the army for part of the day. Bhīma’s duel with Duryodhana ends the open fighting. The attack on the camp follows that night.

bhishma.name: Bhīṣma
bhishma.bio: Śāntanu’s son and the Kuru elder. He gives up the throne, commands Duryodhana’s forces, then teaches Yudhiṣṭhira.

draupadi.name: Draupadī
draupadi.bio: Drupada’s daughter and wife of the five Pāṇḍavas. She challenges the assembly’s authority and shares exile with the brothers.
links: Leaves the court on the last journey

yudhishthira.name: Yudhiṣṭhira
yudhishthira.bio: The eldest Pāṇḍava. He loses his kingdom at dice, becomes king after the war, and faces two tests of loyalty after leaving power.

duryodhana.name: Duryodhana
duryodhana.bio: Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī’s son. He challenges Pāṇḍava rule and refuses Kṛṣṇa’s settlement.

bhima.name: Bhīma
bhima.bio: A Pāṇḍava, brother of Yudhiṣṭhira and Arjuna. He challenges Yudhiṣṭhira in the hall and fights Duryodhana with a mace.

arjuna.name: Arjuna
arjuna.bio: A Pāṇḍava archer. Kṛṣṇa is his charioteer, Abhimanyu is his son, and Droṇa had taught him.
links: Questions fighting his kin and teachers

krishna.name: Kṛṣṇa
krishna.bio: A Yādava ally of the Pāṇḍavas. He moves from envoy to charioteer and counsellor. Gāndhārī later calls him to account.

karna.name: Karṇa
karna.bio: Kuntī’s firstborn, reared away from her. He stands with Duryodhana and eventually takes command. The brothers learn how he is related to them after he dies.
links: Stays with Duryodhana after Kuntī approaches him
Takes charge of the remaining Kaurava forces
Appeals to the rules of combat
The Pāṇḍavas learn he was their eldest brother
Is named among those who attain heaven

vidura.name: Vidura
vidura.bio: A Kuru adviser and the half-brother of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu. He warns the brothers about the house and opposes the use of the dice game.

shakuni.name: Śakuni
shakuni.bio: Gāndhārī’s brother and Duryodhana’s uncle. He plays the dice on Duryodhana’s side.

vikarna.name: Vikarṇa
vikarna.bio: A brother of Duryodhana. At the dice game he defies his own side’s ruling on Draupadī.

drona.name: Droṇa
drona.bio: Teacher of the rival Kuru cousins. He takes command of the Kaurava army after Bhīṣma falls.
links: Stands among Arjuna’s teachers on the other side
His death returns in the final test

shikhandin.name: Śikhaṇḍin
shikhandin.bio: A child of Drupada who fights for the Pāṇḍavas. Bhīṣma refuses to strike Śikhaṇḍin, giving Arjuna an opening.

abhimanyu.name: Abhimanyu
abhimanyu.bio: The son of Arjuna and Subhadrā. His death in the formation prompts Arjuna’s vow.

jayadratha.name: Jayadratha
jayadratha.bio: The Sindhu ruler and husband of Duryodhana’s sister Duḥśalā. He prevents Abhimanyu’s allies from following him.

ashvatthaman.name: Aśvatthāman
ashvatthaman.bio: Droṇa’s son. He survives the main battle and leads the attack on the camp.

gandhari.name: Gāndhārī
gandhari.bio: Mother of Duryodhana and wife of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. After mourning her sons she holds Kṛṣṇa to account and later leaves court.

kunti.name: Kuntī
kunti.bio: Mother of Karṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma and Arjuna. Before the battle she asks Karṇa to join his brothers. She leaves the restored court with the older Kuru couple.
links: Asks Karṇa to join his brothers
Names her firstborn at the water rites

nala.name: Nala
nala.bio: King of Niṣadha in Bṛhadaśva’s story. He loses his kingdom at dice and learns skills that let him recover it.
links: Leaves Damayantī and later reunites with her

damayanti.name: Damayantī
damayanti.bio: A princess of Vidarbha who chooses Nala. She devises a way to bring Nala back within reach after their separation.
